-c: This is the setting people change most. If the server runs out of memory at startup, lower it or leave it unset so auto-fit can choose.
-np: Keep it at 1 if you're the only user, so your chat gets the whole window.
-ngl: If you lower it, context memory for those layers moves to system RAM too. That can fit a bigger context, at reduced speed.
-fit: If you set --ctx-size yourself, auto-fit won't shrink it. With --fit off, a number that's too large can stop the server at startup.
-fitt: The default keeps 1 GB free. A smaller margin allows more context but leaves less for your desktop and other apps.
-kvo: One route to a very large context on a small card: all layers on the GPU, context in system RAM. Expect it to be noticeably slower.
-ctk: Can let more context fit on a small card. Test reply quality if you try it.
-t: The automatic choice is usually fine. Matters little when every layer is on the GPU.
--temp: Check your model's documentation, which often recommends a value.
--min-p: Check your model's documentation, which sometimes recommends turning this off.
-rea: Try off if replies feel slow for simple questions.
--reasoning-effort: The chat template has to support this. The server's /props page lists the template's capabilities.
--reasoning-preserve: Turn it off with --no-reasoning-preserve to make your context window last longer.
--tools: These run with your user account's permissions, so they can read anything you can, including SSH keys. Start with the read-only ones.
--tools-runtime: Use this before you enable shell or file-writing tools.
--host: If you open it to your network, add --api-key too.
--port: Run two servers at once by giving each its own port.
--api-key: Keys on the command line can end up in shell history and process lists. --api-key-file avoids that.
--cors-origins: With the default, any page open in your browser can reach the server. --cors-origins localhost closes that gap, and also stops this site's connection test from working.
--models-dir: This is what makes the web UI's model picker useful. On a small GPU, pair it with --models-max 1.
--spec-type: The ngram types use no extra GPU memory, so they're the easiest to try. They help most when replies repeat existing text, as in code edits.
--spec-draft-model: A draft model needs room in memory too, and helps most on longer outputs.
--embedding: Turning this on stops a chat model from chatting.
--lora: It has to have been trained for the base model you're loading.
--sleep-idle-seconds: Useful if you want your GPU memory back when you aren't chatting.
